chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Why this section exists
Every earlier Part added a table or two as it went, which is the right way to learn a topic but a clumsy way to practice, since rebuilding the whole database means re-reading nine Parts of setup scripts. This section is the single consolidated script: the full schema from Parts 0 to 10 in one place, with seed data restored to a clean, documented starting point (no Part 10 defects still sitting in the tables). Run it on a throwaway database — this is exactly the audience 0.6 described.
## Building it from scratch
If you have been running the scripts from each Part in order, your database already has everything below (once Parts 4, 6, 8 and 10's cleanup scripts have run) — the audit below is just to confirm that. If you're starting fresh, or want a guaranteed-consistent baseline before the exercises, drop and recreate:
```sql
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS hrms_practice;
CREATE DATABASE hrms_practice;
USE hrms_practice;
```

Then run, in order: the Part 0.6 core schema and seed (departments, employees, leave_types, leave_requests, attendance, payroll), Part 7's services/customers/appointments/leave_balances setup, Part 8's ref_payroll_status, employee_documents, the view/trigger/procedure block, and Part 10's company_holidays and leave_status_transitions reference tables (skip Part 10's defect-planting inserts — those exist to be found and cleaned, not to form the baseline). If any of that sounds unfamiliar, it means an earlier Part's script or cleanup wasn't run; the audit query below tells you exactly what's missing.
The consolidated ER overview
| departments ──< employees >── leave_requests >── leave_status_history | │  │                │ | │  │                └──< (self-ref: approved_by → employees) |
|---|---|---|
| │  └──< attendance | │  └──< payroll | │  └──< leave_balances >── leave_types |
| │  └──< employee_documents | │  └──< appointments (as provider) >── appointment_ledger | └── (self-ref: manager_id → employees) |

## customers ──< appointments >── services

(Full detail per table — columns, keys, constraints — is in Appendix E. This is the shape to hold in your head while doing the exercises.)
Audit query: confirm your database matches this baseline
```sql
SELECT 'employees' AS tbl, COUNT(*) AS rows_ FROM employees
```
| UNION ALL SELECT 'departments', COUNT(*) FROM departments | UNION ALL SELECT 'leave_types', COUNT(*) FROM leave_types |
|---|---|
| UNION ALL SELECT 'leave_requests', COUNT(*) FROM leave_requests | UNION ALL SELECT 'leave_status_history', COUNT(*) FROM leave_status_history |
| UNION ALL SELECT 'leave_balances', COUNT(*) FROM leave_balances | UNION ALL SELECT 'attendance', COUNT(*) FROM attendance |
| UNION ALL SELECT 'payroll', COUNT(*) FROM payroll | UNION ALL SELECT 'services', COUNT(*) FROM services |
| UNION ALL SELECT 'customers', COUNT(*) FROM customers | UNION ALL SELECT 'appointments', COUNT(*) FROM appointments |
| UNION ALL SELECT 'employee_documents', COUNT(*) FROM employee_documents | UNION ALL SELECT 'ref_payroll_status', COUNT(*) FROM ref_payroll_status |
| UNION ALL SELECT 'company_holidays', COUNT(*) FROM company_holidays | UNION ALL SELECT 'leave_status_transitions', COUNT(*) FROM leave_status_transitions; |

| tbl                      \| rows_ | employees                \| 5 | departments              \| 4 | leave_types              \| 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| leave_requests           \| 9 | leave_status_history     \| 12 | leave_balances           \| 6 | attendance               \| 8 |
| payroll                  \| 7 | services                 \| 3 | customers                \| 3 | appointments             \| 3 |
| employee_documents       \| 4 | ref_payroll_status       \| 4 | company_holidays         \| 2 | leave_status_transitions \| 5 |

This is the row-count fingerprint the exercises below assume. If your numbers differ, before doing any exercise, work out why — that diagnostic exercise (comparing your actual counts against this table) is itself good practice for 6.1's "reconcile before you trust" habit. A common cause is a Part's demo/defect rows (Part 10's 101+ IDs, for instance) still present; re-run that Part's cleanup script.
## A note on what's deliberately still "messy"
Unlike Part 10's setup, this baseline has no planted defects — every stored value is internally consistent (net pay matches components, approved requests have approvers, history chains are unbroken). This is intentional: the exercises below ask you to write the check first, run it against clean data and confirm zero violations, and then plant a defect yourself and confirm the check catches it — which is precisely the mutation-testing discipline 10.2 taught for validating your own sanity checks, now applied as a learning exercise rather than a one-off habit.

chapters.customSummary:
- Twelve pairs of exercises (two per Part, Parts 1–10), each tagged to the chapter and technique it practices, with collapsible answers.
- Recurring techniques exercised: LEFT JOIN vs INNER JOIN for "include the empty case" (1.1, 4.1); scalar subqueries for aggregate comparisons (2.1, 5.1); DENSE_RANK over LIMIT/OFFSET for tie-safe ranking (2.2, 5.5); conditional COUNT/SUM without join fan-out (3.1, 4.1); self-join pair deduplication with a.id < b.id (4.2); CTE chaining plus ROW_NUMBER "latest per group" (5.1, 5.2, 5.5); EXCEPT for unused-value detection (5.2, 5.4); migration control-total recall (6.1); plant-detect-remove duplicate cycle (6.2, 10.2); idempotent tagged seed/cleanup scripts with children-first deletes (7.1, 7.2, 4.3); CHECK constraint enforcement-vs-acceptance distinction (8.1); schema-to-test-ideas checklist generation (8.2); three-level API assertion structure (9.1); pagination comparison requiring matching ORDER BY/tiebreaker/LIMIT-OFFSET (9.5); attendance and workflow mutation tests (10.1, 10.3, 10.5).
- Answers model one correct approach, not the only one; agreement between differently-written equivalent queries is itself good practice (5.3's cross-check technique).
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## How to use this section
Attempt each exercise against the baseline from 12.1 before reading the answer. Every exercise references the Part and chapter that taught the technique, so if you're stuck, that's exactly where to go back and re-read. Answers are one correct approach, not the only one — if your query returns the same rows by a different route, that's a pass, and comparing why the two forms agree (5.3's two-formulation cross-check) is itself worthwhile practice.
## Part 1 — Database & Query Basics
Exercise 1.1. List every employee's first name, last name and department name, including any employee with no department assigned. Sort by last name.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
```sql
SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name, d.name AS department
FROM   employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id
ORDER  BY e.last_name;
```

LEFT JOIN is required (not JOIN) precisely because the exercise says "including any employee with no department" — see 4.1 for what an INNER JOIN would silently drop.
</details>
Exercise 1.2. Write a query that would fail with "Data too long for column" if you tried to insert a 51-character string into employees.first_name. Don't run it — just write it, and explain in one sentence why it fails.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
```sql
INSERT INTO employees (first_name, last_name, email, hire_date)
VALUES (REPEAT('A', 51), 'Test', 'qa_1.2@example.com', '2026-01-01');
```

It fails because first_name is VARCHAR(50) and, in strict mode, MySQL rejects a value exceeding the declared length rather than silently truncating it (1.2).

| </details> | Part 2 — Filtering & Sorting |
|---|---|
| Exercise 2.1. Find every leave request with a days value strictly greater than the average days across all requests, sorted by days descending. | <details><summary>Answer</summary> |
| SELECT leave_request_id, employee_id, days | FROM   leave_requests |
| WHERE  days > (SELECT AVG(days) FROM leave_requests) | ORDER  BY days DESC; |

Note this can't be written as WHERE days > AVG(days) directly — aggregates aren't allowed in WHERE (3.1), which is exactly why the scalar subquery is needed (5.1).
</details>
Exercise 2.2. Using the baseline data, find the employee(s) with the second-highest total approved leave days. (Hint: LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 is tempting but wrong if there's a tie for first — think about why, per 2.2 and 5.5.)
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
```sql
WITH totals AS (
  SELECT employee_id, SUM(days) AS total_days
  FROM   leave_requests WHERE status = 'approved'
  GROUP  BY employee_id
```
| ), | ranked AS ( |
|---|---|
| SELECT employee_id, total_days, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_days DESC) AS rnk | FROM   totals |
| ) | SELECT employee_id, total_days FROM ranked WHERE rnk = 2; |

DENSE_RANK (5.5) handles ties correctly; LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 would silently skip a tied second-place employee if two people shared the top total, since it counts rows, not distinct rank positions.

| </details> | Part 3 — Aggregation |
|---|---|
| Exercise 3.1. For each department, show the count of active employees and the count of all employees (including inactive/resigned), in one query, without double-counting via a join to leave_requests. | <details><summary>Answer</summary> |
| SELECT d.name, | SUM(e.status = 'active' AND e.is_deleted = 0) AS active_count, |
| COUNT(e.employee_id)                          AS total_count | FROM   departments d |
| LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.department_id | GROUP  BY d.department_id, d.name; |

COUNT(e.employee_id) rather than COUNT(*) avoids the "empty department shows 1" trap from 4.1; SUM(boolean expression) is the conditional-count pattern from 3.1.
</details>
Exercise 3.2. Find every (employee_id, pay_month) combination that appears more than once in payroll — trick question, using the clean baseline. What should this return, and why is that itself worth confirming?
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
```sql
SELECT employee_id, pay_month, COUNT(*) FROM payroll GROUP BY employee_id, pay_month HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
```

Zero rows, because the baseline has no planted duplicate (unlike Part 3's original teaching data, which deliberately had one). Confirming an empty result on clean data — rather than just assuming it — is the "prove the check can pass" half of the mutation-testing discipline from 10.2; the other half is exercise 6.3 below, where you plant one on purpose.
</details>
## Part 4 — Joins
Exercise 4.1. List every department alongside its employee count, including departments with zero employees.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
```sql
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.employee_id) AS staff
FROM   departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.department_id
GROUP  BY d.department_id, d.name;
```

"Legal" (department_id 4, from Part 4's own setup — drop it first if you ran that Part's cleanup, or re-add it to see the zero-row case) is the department this pattern is built to surface; COUNT(e.employee_id), not COUNT(*), is what makes zero show correctly (4.1).
</details>
Exercise 4.2. Find every pair of employees who report to the same manager, listing each pair once (not twice, and not paired with themselves).
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
```sql
SELECT a.first_name AS person_a, b.first_name AS person_b
FROM   employees a JOIN employees b ON a.manager_id = b.manager_id AND a.employee_id < b.employee_id;
```

The a.employee_id < b.employee_id condition is the self-join deduplication trick from 4.2; employees with manager_id IS NULL are correctly excluded since NULL = NULL isn't true.

| </details> | Part 5 — Subqueries, CTEs & Set Operations |
|---|---|
| Exercise 5.1. Using a CTE, find each employee's most recent leave request (by start_date), and alongside it, show how many total requests that employee has made. | <details><summary>Answer</summary> |
| WITH totals AS ( | SELECT employee_id, COUNT(*) AS total_requests FROM leave_requests GROUP BY employee_id |
| ), | latest AS ( |
| SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY start_date DESC, leave_request_id DESC) AS rn | FROM   leave_requests |
| ) | SELECT l.employee_id, l.leave_request_id, l.start_date, t.total_requests |
| FROM   latest l JOIN totals t ON t.employee_id = l.employee_id | WHERE  l.rn = 1; |

Combines the CTE-chaining pattern (5.2) with the ROW_NUMBER "latest per group" pattern (5.5); the tiebreaker (leave_request_id DESC) guarantees exactly one row per employee even on a tied start_date.
</details>
Exercise 5.2. Using EXCEPT, find any leave type listed in leave_types that has never been used in a single leave_requests row.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>
```sql
SELECT leave_type_id FROM leave_types
```
EXCEPT
```sql
SELECT DISTINCT leave_type_id FROM leave_requests;
```

On the baseline this returns nothing (both leave types are used); the exercise is worth re-running after adding a third, unused leave type to see it fire — exactly the "prove it can fail" step from 10.2, applied here to a set-operator query.
</details>
## Part 6 — Data Validation Techniques for QA
Exercise 6.1. Write the row-count and control-total comparison for legacy_employees versus mig_employees from 6.1's migration scenario, from memory, without looking back at the chapter. Then check your answer against 6.1.
<details><summary>Answer</summary> This is intentionally a recall exercise, not a new pattern — the value is in reconstructing the `UNION ALL` with `row_cnt`, `total_salary`, `min_date`/`max_date` and `distinct_emails` from memory, then noticing (as 6.1 emphasized) that matching row counts alone would have hidden both the duplicate and the missing employee. </details>
Exercise 6.2. On the clean Part 12 baseline, plant one duplicate payroll row for employee 1 in month 2026-07-01 (same values as the existing row, new payroll_id), then write the check that finds it, confirm it fires, then remove the planted row and confirm the check goes quiet again.

| <details><summary>Answer</summary> | -- plant |
|---|---|
| INSERT INTO payroll (employee_id, pay_month, basic_salary, allowances, deductions, net_pay, status) | SELECT employee_id, pay_month, basic_salary, allowances, deductions, net_pay, status |

-- check (10.2's PAY-02)
```sql
SELECT employee_id, pay_month, COUNT(*) FROM payroll GROUP BY employee_id, pay_month HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
-- should return exactly one row: (1, '2026-07-01', 2)
```

-- remove and reconfirm
```sql
DELETE FROM payroll WHERE payroll_id = (SELECT MAX(payroll_id) FROM payroll);
```

This is 10.2's "test your checks" discipline done by hand once, so the habit sticks before you automate it.

| </details> | Part 7 — DML, DDL & Test Data |
|---|---|
| Exercise 7.1. Write a safely tagged, idempotent seed script (7.2's pattern) that creates one employee tagged qa_ex7_, gives them a leave balance, then a cleanup script that removes exactly that employee and their balance, children first. | <details><summary>Answer</summary> |
| -- seed | INSERT INTO employees (first_name, last_name, email, department_id, hire_date, status) |
| SELECT 'QA_Ex7', 'Tester', 'qa_ex7_tester@example.com', 2, '2025-01-01', 'active' | WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees WHERE email = 'qa_ex7_tester@example.com'); |

SET @emp := (SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE email = 'qa_ex7_tester@example.com');
```sql
INSERT INTO leave_balances (employee_id, leave_type_id, balance)
SELECT @emp, 1, 18.0 WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM leave_balances WHERE employee_id = @emp AND leave_type_id = 1);
```

-- cleanup (children first)
```sql
DELETE FROM leave_balances WHERE employee_id = (SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE email = 'qa_ex7_tester@example.com');
DELETE FROM employees WHERE email = 'qa_ex7_tester@example.com';
```

The WHERE NOT EXISTS guards make both inserts safe to run twice — exactly the idempotency requirement from 7.2.
</details>
Exercise 7.2. Explain, without running it, why DELETE FROM employees WHERE email = 'qa_ex7_tester@example.com' alone (skipping the leave_balances delete) would fail on this schema, and what error you'd see.
<details><summary>Answer</summary> It would fail with MySQL error 1451 (`Cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key constraint fails`), because `leave_balances.employee_id` has a foreign key referencing `employees.employee_id`, and a row still references the employee being deleted (4.3, 7.1's "children first" rule). </details>
## Part 8 — Constraints & Schema Awareness
Exercise 8.1. Without running it, predict what happens if you INSERT INTO leave_requests (employee_id, leave_type_id, start_date, end_date, days, status) VALUES (1, 1, '2026-06-01', '2026-06-01', -1, 'pending') — assuming Part 8's chk_leave_days constraint is present. What if it isn't (e.g., you're on MySQL 8.0.15)?
<details><summary>Answer</summary> With the constraint present and enforced (MySQL 8.0.16+): rejected with error 3819 (`Check constraint 'chk_leave_days' is violated`), since `-1` fails `days > 0`. Without enforcement (older MySQL): the statement succeeds and a nonsensical `-1`-day request is silently stored — exactly 8.1's warning that `CHECK` syntax being *accepted* doesn't mean it's being *enforced*, and why a real negative-value insert test (not just reading the DDL) is the only way to be sure. </details>
Exercise 8.2. Read employee_documents' DDL (SHOW CREATE TABLE employee_documents) and, without consulting 8.2 again, list at least five distinct test ideas it implies.
<details><summary>Answer</summary> Expected ideas: `doc_type` enum boundary (each value plus an invalid one); the `(employee_id, doc_type)` unique-among-active-rows behavior from 8.4's soft-delete trap (create, soft-delete, recreate, second-active-should-fail); `created_by` nullable (Mina's certificate has none in the Part 8 setup — a real example already in your data); `updated_at ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` side effects; FK to `employees` (orphan/missing-parent test). Five or more of these, independently arrived at, is the exercise's real point — 8.2's checklist-generation query is a shortcut for arriving at the same list mechanically. </details>
## Part 9 — SQL in API/Backend Testing
Exercise 9.1. Sketch (pseudocode is fine) a test that POSTs a new leave request via an API, then verifies three things at three different levels, per 9.1's three-level assertion structure.
<details><summary>Answer</summary> Level 1 (response contract): status is 201, body has an `id` and `status: "pending"`. Level 2 (persisted state): a `SELECT` on `leave_requests` by that `id` returns exactly the submitted `employee_id`/`start_date`/`end_date`/`days`. Level 3 (unmentioned side effect): a `SELECT COUNT(*)` on `leave_status_history` for that request's id, with `new_status = 'pending'`, equals 1 — a side effect the API response body never mentions but the trigger from 8.3 guarantees. </details>
Exercise 9.2. Why is WHERE status IN ('pending') alone insufficient to validate a paginated GET /leave-requests?status=pending&page=2&pageSize=3 endpoint? What two additional things does the comparison query need?
<details><summary>Answer</summary> It needs the same `ORDER BY` (with a unique tiebreaker) and the matching `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` for that specific page — otherwise you're comparing "all pending requests" against "page 2 of pending requests," which will almost never match by row count alone, let alone by identity (9.5). </details>
## Part 10 — Practical QA Query Patterns
Exercise 10.1. Using only the clean 12.1 baseline (no Part 10 defects), run the attendance integrity scoreboard from 10.3. Confirm every check returns zero. Then manually insert one row that violates ATT-05 (a punch on a Saturday) and re-run just that one check to confirm it fires.
<details><summary>Answer</summary> On the clean baseline, all eight `ATT-` checks from 10.3 should return 0. After inserting, say, `INSERT INTO attendance (employee_id, work_date, check_in, check_out) VALUES (1, '2026-09-26', '09:00:00', '17:00:00')` (a Saturday), `ATT-05`'s `WEEKDAY(a.work_date) >= 5` condition should return 1. This exercise is the attendance-module instance of the same mutation-testing habit exercised in 12.2's exercise 6.2 for payroll. </details>
Exercise 10.2. Write the WFL-001 illegal-transition check from 10.5 as a standalone query, run it against the clean baseline (expect zero rows), then insert a history row that represents rejected → approved for any existing request, and confirm it's caught.
<details><summary>Answer</summary> This reuses the exact query from 10.5's "Illegal transitions in the history" section. On clean baseline data: zero rows (no such transition exists once Part 10's own planted defect on request 7 has been cleaned up, per that Part's cleanup script). Planting `INSERT INTO leave_status_history (leave_request_id, old_status, new_status, changed_by, changed_at) VALUES (6, 'rejected', 'approved', 1, NOW())` and re-running should surface exactly that row, since `('rejected', 'approved')` has no matching row in `leave_status_transitions`. </details>

chapters.customSummary:
- Brief: build a complete, reusable sanity-check suite for one module (leave recommended; payroll or appointments as alternatives) end to end, assembling techniques from all twelve Parts rather than following a handed-down answer.
- Eight-part deliverable checklist: (1) a plain-English rules document with made-up requirement IDs; (2) 8+ individually written check queries in 10.2's header format, returning violating rows; (3) a UNION ALL scoreboard; (4) a baseline file with at least one dated, reasoned accepted exception; (5) a runnable runner (SQL procedure or pytest/Node, per 9.2/9.4); (6) mutation tests proving at least three checks can actually fail; (7) one full investigation write-up in 11.3's template format, from a real (possibly self-planted) anomaly; (8) a README covering how to run, extend, and interpret severity.
- Suggested build order follows the checklist top to bottom, each step depending on the last; step 8 (documentation) is the most-skipped and most-valuable step.
- Done-criteria: clean baseline passes cleanly, re-running Part 10's defect-planting catches every planted issue, and the investigation write-up is developer-ready without further editing — the same bar 10.2 set for a production suite, scoped to one module.
- Extending to a second module reveals shared structural patterns (duplicate detection, orphan anti-joins, status/history reconciliation) across tables, the natural path from a one-off exercise toward the reusable, cross-module library 10.2 and 10.5 were building toward.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
The brief
Pick one module — leave is recommended, since it's the most fully worked example across this manual, but payroll or appointments work equally well if you'd rather practice on material you've seen a little less of. Build a complete, reusable sanity-check suite for it, following every practice this manual has built toward, end to end. This section describes the deliverable; it deliberately doesn't hand you the finished answer, since assembling it yourself, from techniques you've now practiced individually across twelve Parts, is the actual exercise.
## Deliverable checklist
Your suite should include all of the following, each one traceable to the chapter that taught it:
A rules document, in plain English, one line per rule, each with a made-up-but-plausible requirement ID (6.1's mapping-spec habit, 10.2's "source" field). For leave, this means writing out — in your own words, not copied from 10.4/10.5 — the working-week rule, the overlap rule, the balance rule, and the legal state-transition table.
At least eight individual check queries, each following 10.2's header format exactly (id, rule, source, severity, owner, params, returns), each returning violating rows, not just a count. Draw from the families in 10.1 (impossible values, contradictions, absence) and the specific leave templates in 10.4 and 10.5 — but write them yourself rather than copy-pasting, since the retyping is what cements the pattern.
A scoreboard query that UNION ALLs all eight-plus checks into the one-row-per-rule report format from 10.2 and 10.3.
A baseline file (YAML or a table, per 10.2) with at least one deliberately accepted known issue, a reason, and an expiry date — even if you have to plant that one issue yourself to have something legitimate to baseline.
A runner, in whichever tool you're most comfortable with (10.2's SQL stored-procedure runner, or a pytest/Node runner per 9.2 and 9.4) — it must support running the whole suite in one command and reporting pass/fail per check against the baseline.
Mutation tests for at least three of your checks: for each, a short script that plants the violation inside a rolled-back transaction, confirms the check fires, and rolls back — proving each check can actually fail, per 10.2's "test your checks" section.
One full investigation write-up, in the format from 11.3's closing section (summary, query, full result, severity, hypothesis, "what fixed looks like"), for whichever real anomaly your suite turns up when run against data you've deliberately made messy — either by re-running Part 10's defect-planting inserts, or by inventing your own new ones.
A short README explaining how to run the suite, how to add a new check, and what each severity level means for your project (10.2's "keeping the library healthy" section).
## Suggested build order
Work top to bottom through the checklist above; each step depends on the one before it. Steps 1–3 are pure SQL and can be done in any client (11.1). Step 4 is a text file. Step 5 is where you pick a language and framework, informed by 9.2's comparison table. Steps 6–7 are where the suite proves itself against real (planted) defects, exactly mirroring the individual mutation-test exercises in 12.2. Step 8 is the part most people skip and shouldn't — a suite nobody else can run or extend has limited value beyond your own single use of it, per 10.2's closing point about ownership.
## How to know you're done
Run your finished suite against the clean 12.1 baseline: every check should pass (or match its baseline exactly). Then re-run Part 10's defect-planting inserts for your chosen module and run the suite again: every planted defect should be caught by at least one check, and the investigation write-up from step 7 should read as something you could genuinely hand to a developer without further editing. That combination — clean data passes, known-bad data is fully caught, and the evidence is self-contained — is the same bar 10.2 set for a production sanity suite, just scoped to one module and built by hand instead of inherited from a team.
## Where to go from here
A finished mini-project is, in miniature, exactly what 10.2 described teams maintaining in production: owned, dated, tested, and growing by one check per bug found. If you extend it to a second module, you'll notice several of your checks (duplicate-key detection, orphan anti-joins, status/history reconciliation) are structurally identical to the first module's, just pointed at different tables — which is itself the observation that turns a one-off suite into the kind of reusable, cross-module sanity library 10.2 and 10.5 were building toward all along.
